explainedBy: The investor points to the target quarterly acceleration threshold of 25 to 50 percent minimum.

storyboard.claim: Quarterly earnings must accelerate by at least 25 to 50 percent.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor sits at his workstation pointing to a target metric icon representing the strict earnings cutoff.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens Chunk 2 by quantifying the explosive earnings acceleration baseline.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the minimum threshold target that separates true market leaders from mediocre stocks.

explainedBy: The investor rejects the illusion of a single windfall quarter from non-operational sales.
noVisual: Non-operating windfalls like real estate sales cannot be drawn directly without confusing the trading context.

storyboard.claim: A single lucky quarter from asset sales does not count as real growth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation speaks firmly beside the struck-through phrase crossing out the lucky quarter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Disqualifies temporary earnings spikes from the legitimate acceleration defined in beat 38.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike visually eliminates one-time windfalls from valid CAN SLIM candidates.

explainedBy: A flow diagram links the current quarterly earnings surge with three consecutive years of annual growth.

storyboard.claim: Annual earnings growth over three years must validate the current quarter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-stage flow diagram showing CURRENT QUARTER flowing into 3-YEAR GROWTH.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Builds the dual-filter foundation by adding the multi-year track record to the current quarter.
storyboard.addedInformation: Abstracts the pairing mechanism into an explicit analytical sequence.

explainedBy: The flow diagram resolves into a third stage showing how historical proof and current acceleration produce an explosive spark.

storyboard.claim: The collision of annual proof and quarterly acceleration sparks the stock's major run.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow diagram extends with a third node labeled EXPLOSIVE SPARK receiving input from the first two.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the flow sequence started in beat 40 by revealing the ultimate outcome.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the causal synergy where historical track record and immediate momentum converge.

explainedBy: The investor consults O'Neil's historical records book to examine the 1958 Texas Instruments case study.

storyboard.claim: O'Neil grounds CAN SLIM rules in historical winners like Texas Instruments in 1958.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor in a study room holding a book of market models with the historical case study callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the theoretical formula to a concrete historical case study.
storyboard.addedInformation: Anchors the discussion in documented market history rather than speculation.

explainedBy: The investor examines company figures through a magnifier, demonstrating intense analytical discipline.

storyboard.claim: The real discipline is rigorously scrutinizing earnings deceleration before the crowd notices.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation holds a magnifier up to examine the fine print of financial reports.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from identifying the company to the discipline needed to monitor its growth trajectory.
storyboard.addedInformation: The magnifier highlights the forensic scrutiny required to spot early warning signs.

explainedBy: The investor highlights the blistering initial earnings numbers driving Texas Instruments' historic run.

storyboard.claim: Texas Instruments began its historic advance with blistering earnings growth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation reviews the surging performance metrics displayed on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Establishes the explosive growth baseline before the subsequent slowdown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the initial euphoria and validation of early CAN SLIM criteria.

explainedBy: The investor points to the remarkable quarterly growth sequence of 129, 97, and 87 percent as it begins to moderate.

storyboard.claim: Growth rates peaked at 129 percent before beginning a visible downshift.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor remains at the workstation pointing to the descending growth rate numbers.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the workstation inspection by displaying the specific numerical peak.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the exact inflection point where triple-digit growth begins to cool.

explainedBy: The investor reacts with concern to two consecutive quarters of growth slowing to 22 percent.

storyboard.claim: Growth sharply decelerated to 22 percent across two back-to-back quarters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at the same workstation looks concerned as the quarterly growth drop is highlighted.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the confirmation of deceleration following the peak shown in beat 45.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shifts the emotional and analytical tone from excitement to danger.

explainedBy: The investor notes the deceptive nuance where positive absolute earnings conceal slowing growth.
noVisual: The mathematical distinction between positive levels and negative second derivatives is conceptual.

storyboard.claim: Positive total profits trick most people into ignoring slowing growth velocity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor speaks directly at the workstation, highlighting the common analytical trap.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pauses to emphasize why most traders fail to act on the deceleration shown in beat 46.
storyboard.addedInformation: warns the viewer against confusing nominal profitability with accelerating momentum.

explainedBy: The institutional analyst smugly advises holding the stock while the retail investor looks skeptical.

storyboard.claim: Wall Street urges holding mature profitable companies despite their slowing growth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager speaks smugly next to a struck-through HOLD ON TO IT callout, while the investor stands skeptical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts mainstream analyst complacency with the quantitative warning sign.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike rejects standard Wall Street advice to hold slowing winners.

explainedBy: The investor slumps in dread as the growth collapse from 129 percent to 20 percent acts as an alarm.

storyboard.claim: The sudden deceleration from 129 percent down to 20 percent is a critical warning alarm.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps at his desk under high tension with an alarm callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Translates the analytical slowdown into an urgent emergency for the trader.
storyboard.addedInformation: Dramatizes the urgency of the growth drop that analysts dismissed in beat 48.

explainedBy: The investor walks away from the trade, executing the mathematical rule to sell as momentum expires.

storyboard.claim: Deceleration is the objective mathematical mandate to exit the position.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor walks decisively away from the trading desk, concluding the Texas Instruments case.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Resolves the Texas Instruments sequence with the definitive exit action.
storyboard.addedInformation: Demonstrates strict mechanical execution over emotional attachment.

explainedBy: The retail investor pushes back anxiously while the institutional host calmly welcomes the objection.

storyboard.claim: Retail traders instinctively fear that buying explosive growth is reckless.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor gestures in panic as the institutional host smirks back confidently.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the case study to an interactive devil's advocate debate.
storyboard.addedInformation: Captures the visceral psychological recoil most people feel toward buying high growth.

explainedBy: The investor questions whether requiring massive growth forces traders into unsustainable bubbles.
noVisual: A financial bubble cannot be drawn as a literal soap bubble without trivializing the market risk.

storyboard.claim: Demanding extreme growth rates seems like an invitation to buy financial bubbles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor argues the objection with an anxious expression beside the bubble callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Articulates the specific argument behind the skepticism raised in beat 51.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the classic retail critique of momentum and growth investing.

explainedBy: The investor presses the point that chasing unsustainable growth means buying at the absolute peak of hype.
noVisual: Metaphors like trees growing to the sky read literally and mislead viewers; the hype concept is text-carried.

storyboard.claim: Skeptics argue that high growth requirements lead straight into peak hype.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points upward emphatically, challenging the wisdom of chasing peak valuations.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens the counter-argument before the rebuttal begins.
storyboard.addedInformation: Identifies the fear of buying the exact top of an unsustainable advance.

explainedBy: The institutional manager explains that the objection fundamentally misunderstands the trader's true objective.

storyboard.claim: The objection fails to understand that CAN SLIM traders never plan to hold forever.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager speaks patiently while the retail investor listens attentively.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the formal refutation of the devil's advocate argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Validates the skeptic's premise while shifting to the correct tactical framework.

explainedBy: The trader rejects romantic lifelong attachment to a corporation.
noVisual: Marriage and romance icons would mislead viewers into reading literal romance.

storyboard.claim: Traders must abandon the buy-and-hold romantic attachment to companies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor firmly gestures no beside the struck-through phrase MARRYING THIS COMPANY.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Dismantles the conventional investing myth of holding beloved companies forever.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strips away emotional sentimentality from stock ownership.

explainedBy: The investor targets the precise mathematical window of hyper-acceleration on his charts.

storyboard.claim: Stocks should only be held during the precise mathematical window of hyper-acceleration.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation points to the target icon framing the specific trading window.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the positive replacement strategy to the romantic myth rejected in beat 55.
storyboard.addedInformation: Focuses capital exclusively on periods of maximum velocity.

explainedBy: The investor steps away down the road before deceleration causes a catastrophic derailment.

storyboard.claim: Two quarters of deceleration require stepping off before the position derails.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor executes a leave action walking past the road icon representing the exit path.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Details the concrete exit trigger that enforces the temporary holding strategy.
storyboard.addedInformation: Translates mathematical deceleration into a definitive physical departure.

explainedBy: The investor consciously dismisses the psychological craving for comfortable mediocre growth.
noVisual: Psychological comfort and complacency are mental states lacking direct physical icons.

storyboard.claim: Investors must suppress the instinct to seek comfort in slow 12 percent growers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor speaks with clear resolve beside the struck-through callout rejecting comfortable stocks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly links back to the psychological barrier that blocks explosive returns.
storyboard.addedInformation: Eliminates the false security of average returns from the trader's mindset.

explainedBy: A spectrum diagram contrasts safe and steady against explosive acceleration, showing where market rewards concentrate.

storyboard.claim: The market heavily rewards explosive acceleration over safe and steady stocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum diagram placing the value indicator near the explosive acceleration pole.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Summarizes the entire C & A debate with a clear quantitative spectrum.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visually polarizes the two investing philosophies and highlights the asymmetric payoff.

explainedBy: The investor holds a lightbulb, introducing the new catalyst and new highs that trigger acceleration.

storyboard.claim: The N in CAN SLIM stands for new catalysts that trigger explosive acceleration.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation holds an illuminating lightbulb icon symbolizing a new catalyst.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from earnings metrics (C and A) to the operational catalyst (N).
storyboard.addedInformation: Provides a concrete symbol for the spark that drives institutional interest.

explainedBy: The institutional manager emphasizes that only a massive shift in business reality causes explosive growth.
noVisual: A macroeconomic or corporate operational overhaul is systemic and lacks a single physical motif.

storyboard.claim: Explosive earnings require a structural transformation in underlying operations.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager speaks from his trading office highlighting the operational change.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the underlying cause behind the catalyst introduced in beat 60.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reminds the trader that charts reflect real underlying business transformations.

explainedBy: The investor studies the historical notes documenting Wright Aeronautical in 1927.

storyboard.claim: Wright Aeronautical in 1927 provides the classic historical study of a new catalyst.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor in the study room reviews archival notes on the 1927 aviation breakthrough.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Grounds the catalyst concept in a legendary historical market case.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the narrative example that will demonstrate catalysts and all-time highs.

explainedBy: The observer reacts in awe to the deafening roar and power of the industrial factory floor.
noVisual: Smell of ozone and loud factory noise cannot be drawn visually in the rig.

storyboard.claim: The factory floor was an intensely sensory environment of deafening industrial production.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor covers his ears or reacts with astonishment against an abstract industrial backdrop.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transports the viewer into the physical manufacturing reality behind the breakthrough.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sensory immersion contrasting raw physical engineering with Wall Street ticker screens.

explainedBy: The investor points to the chess knight icon celebrating the revolutionary aircraft engine as a total game changer.

storyboard.claim: The air-cooled aircraft engine was a revolutionary technological game changer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor points to the chess knight game icon signifying a decisive strategic breakthrough.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the specific physical innovation that produced the factory roar in beat 63.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chess knight emphasizes the game-changing strategic leap in aviation.

explainedBy: The institutional manager on Wall Street monitors the frantically chattering ticker tape feed.

storyboard.claim: On Wall Street, the ticker tape exploded with furious trading activity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional trader on a busy trading floor reacts to rapid incoming market tape.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts from the factory floor innovation to the Wall Street market reaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the institutional transmission mechanism turning technological disruption into trading frenzy.

explainedBy: The institutional manager celebrates as Wright Aeronautical breaks out to an absolute all-time high.

storyboard.claim: Wright Aeronautical surged to an unprecedented all-time high price.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager celebrates in his office beside the all-time high callout.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the price consequence of the frantic ticker tape buying in beat 65.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the critical price milestone that terrifies retail traders.

explainedBy: The retail investor freezes in terror, refusing to buy a stock trading at all-time highs.

storyboard.claim: Retail traders are terrified to buy stocks trading at all-time record highs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The retail investor slumps fearfully at his desk, paralyzed by the high stock price.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly contrasts the institutional celebration in beat 66 with retail paralysis.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the psychological fallacy that what is high cannot go higher.

explainedBy: The investor rejects buying stagnant, comfortable stocks that linger at five-year-old price levels.

storyboard.claim: Traders must avoid buying stagnant stocks that remain stuck at multi-year lows.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor turns away from the struck-through phrase rejecting old comfortable stocks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Points out the negative habit that leads retail traders to avoid winning stocks.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike discredits the false comfort of buying unmoving legacy stocks.

explainedBy: A sorter diagram categorizes the three main market catalysts: new product, new management, and new industry conditions.

storyboard.claim: New catalysts fall into three primary categories: products, management, or industry conditions.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-bucket sorter diagram displaying NEW PRODUCT, NEW MANAGEMENT, and NEW CONDITION.
storyboard.onScreenText: NEW PRODUCT | NEW MANAGEMENT | NEW CONDITION
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Breaks down the broad catalyst concept into its three concrete operational forms.
storyboard.addedInformation: Organizes the diverse triggers that can ignite explosive institutional buying.

explainedBy: The investor examines historical market records illustrating the 1970s energy crisis as a catalyst.

storyboard.claim: The 1970s energy crisis created a massive industry condition catalyst for Dome Petroleum.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his workstation holds research notes detailing the energy crisis catalyst.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Provides a concrete historical example of the third sorter bucket (industry conditions).
storyboard.addedInformation: Validates macroeconomic and commodity shifts as valid CAN SLIM triggers.

explainedBy: The investor celebrates the massive 1,000 percent advance generated by the new fundamental catalyst.

storyboard.claim: Dome advanced 1,000 percent powered by the fundamental energy of the new catalyst.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor raises his hands celebrating the monumental 1,000 percent return on his chart.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Demonstrates the spectacular payoff of correctly identifying a new industry catalyst.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reinforces the massive magnitude of gains possible when catalysts align.

explainedBy: The investor wrestles with the difficult requirement of buying stocks breaking out into new all-time high territory.

storyboard.claim: Traders find buying stocks at brand new price highs the most difficult rule to accept.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor at his trading desk speaks with visible anxiety about buying at record price highs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the operational catalyst to the psychological dread of new highs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Highlights the emotional resistance that keeps most traders from buying winning stocks.

explainedBy: The institutional manager introduces the mechanics of overhead supply and trapped buyer psychology.

storyboard.claim: Overhead supply is a mechanical price barrier driven by trapped buyer psychology.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The institutional manager gestures explanatory to the investor in the office setting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets up the psychological explanation for why new highs offer frictionless advance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Deconstructs a seemingly technical concept into raw human emotion.

explainedBy: The retail investor slumps in horror beside the crash icon as his $50 stock plummets to $20.

storyboard.claim: Buying at fifty dollars before a crash to twenty traps the investor in severe pain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor slumps at his desk beside the red crash icon showing the collapse from fifty to twenty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Instantiates the trapped buyer scenario with concrete prices and sudden disaster.
storyboard.addedInformation: Visualizes the traumatic origin of overhead supply.

explainedBy: The investor slumps in exhaustion after holding a losing stock for five agonizing years.

storyboard.claim: Five years of holding a collapsed stock erodes all desire for profit into pure regret.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor remains slumped at his workstation, burdened by five years of trapped capital.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Depicts the prolonged psychological wear of bag-holding through the years.
storyboard.addedInformation: Emphasizes how time transforms an aggressive growth expectation into desperate regret.

explainedBy: The trapped investor vows to sell the instant the stock recovers to fifty dollars to get his money back.

storyboard.claim: Trapped buyers only want to break even at fifty dollars and dump their shares.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The investor speaks with desperate relief at his desk, ready to sell the moment the stock hits fifty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the trapped buyer narrative, establishing the exact mechanism that forms overhead resistance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reveals the psychological origin of overhead supply before chunk 3 explores its market impact.
